explanations.explanation: Shiloh it is, friend. The whole congregation of Israel assembles there and sets up the Tent of Meeting (Joshua 18:1). Every tribe in one place, and everybody knows where to look for the Tent. That's a gathering with a clear address.

Gilgal sounds like a solid guess, but this gathering happens somewhere else. The text says the whole congregation assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there (Joshua 18:1). So the Tent has a new spot, and the whole crowd shows up to it.

Hebron is a real place in this book, friend, but it's not where this crowd gathers. The text says the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there (Joshua 18:1). Shiloh is where the Tent goes up and where the big moment is about to happen.

explanations.answer: Seven tribes haven't received their inheritance
explanations.explanation: That's the loose end, friend. Even though the land is subdued before them, there are still seven tribes of Israel who haven't yet received their inheritance (Joshua 18:1-2). Winning the land is one thing. Handing it out is another. Seven tribes are still standing there with empty hands.

explanations.answer: The Tent of Meeting has no priest
explanations.explanation: The Tent just went up at Shiloh, and nothing in the text says it's missing a priest. What the text does say is that seven tribes of Israel had not yet received their inheritance (Joshua 18:2). That's the unfinished business. The Tent is ready, but the land still has to be handed out.

Walls never come up here, friend. Judah already has its land at this point. The problem is that seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance (Joshua 18:2). So the question is who's still waiting, not what needs building.

Careful, friend, it's the other way around. Joshua doesn't ask why they're in a hurry. He asks, "How long will you put off entering and possessing the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?" (Joshua 18:3). He's asking why they're dragging their feet, not why they're rushing.

False is right, friend. Nobody's rushing here. Joshua asks, "How long will you put off entering and possessing the land that the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?" (Joshua 18:3). The land is a gift already given, and he wants to know why they're still waiting.

Three men from each tribe, just like Joshua says (Joshua 18:4). Seven tribes still waiting means a whole crowd of mapmakers heading out. I think that's a lot of pairs of eyes, and nobody gets lost alone. Three is the number, friend.
Ten would make for a very crowded survey, friend. Joshua says to appoint three men from each tribe (Joshua 18:4). With seven tribes waiting, that's plenty of people already. Small teams, big map.

Twelve is a famous number in Israel, so I get why it jumped out. But Joshua asks for three men from each tribe (Joshua 18:4). Twelve men per tribe would be a traffic jam on the map. Three each, friend.

explanations.answer: Survey the land and map it out
explanations.explanation: That's the job. Joshua says he will send them out "to survey the land and map it out, according to the inheritance of each" (Joshua 18:4). No swords this time, just eyes, notes and a whole lot of walking. They come back, and then the land can be divided into seven portions.

explanations.answer: Drive the Canaanites out of it
explanations.explanation: That's not the assignment here, friend. The land is already subdued before them (Joshua 18:1). Joshua sends the men out to survey the land and map it out (Joshua 18:4). This trip is about mapping, not fighting.

explanations.answer: Build an altar in every region
explanations.explanation: No altar-building in this plan, friend. Joshua tells them they'll "survey the land and map it out" (Joshua 18:4). They're mapmakers on this trip. Nothing in the plan mentions altars.

Lots, friend. Joshua says, "I will cast lots for you here in the presence of the LORD our God" (Joshua 18:6). No arguing over who gets what, and no tribe picking its favorite view. It's all decided right there in the LORD's presence.

explanations.answer: Give the biggest tribe first pick
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets first pick based on size, friend. Joshua says, "I will cast lots for you here in the presence of the LORD our God" (Joshua 18:6). The portions are mapped out first, then the lots decide. Big tribe or small tribe, same method.

The mapmakers do the walking, but they don't do the choosing. Joshua says he will cast lots for them "here in the presence of the LORD our God" (Joshua 18:6). The men bring back the map, and the lots take it from there.

Priesthood, friend. Joshua says the Levites have no portion among them "because their inheritance is the priesthood of the LORD" (Joshua 18:7). They don't get a slice of land like the others. What they get is serving the LORD.

A mountain would at least be something to point at, friend. But Joshua says the Levites' inheritance is "the priesthood of the LORD" (Joshua 18:7). That's why they have no portion of land among the tribes.

Harvest sounds like it fits with land, friend, but that's not what the text says. Joshua says the Levites have no portion because "their inheritance is the priesthood of the LORD" (Joshua 18:7). Their inheritance is the priesthood, not a crop.

True, friend. Joshua says Gad, Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh have already received the inheritance that Moses the servant of the LORD gave them beyond the Jordan to the east (Joshua 18:7). Their land is already settled. So they're not waiting in this drawing.

This one is true, friend. Joshua says Gad, Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh "have already received the inheritance that Moses the servant of the LORD gave them beyond the Jordan to the east" (Joshua 18:7). Their land is already handed out. That's why they're not in this drawing.

A document, friend. The men went throughout the land, mapping it city by city into seven portions, then returned with the document to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh (Joshua 18:9). Seven portions, all written down. Now Joshua has something in hand to cast lots over.

explanations.answer: A count of every fighting man
explanations.explanation: No headcount this time, friend. The men were sent to map the land, and they returned with the document to Joshua (Joshua 18:9). The map is what they carry back. Nothing in the text mentions counting soldiers.

Gift baskets would've been a nice touch, friend, but the text doesn't mention any. The men went throughout the land, mapping it city by city, and returned with the document to Joshua (Joshua 18:9). The document is what they bring back.

Joshua son of Nun, friend, the very man running this whole land-dividing operation. The Israelites gave him an inheritance among them when they had finished distributing the land (Joshua 19:49). He handled everybody else's portion first, and his came after.

Eleazar, the priest, is right there at the distribution, friend. But the one who receives the extra inheritance is Joshua son of Nun (Joshua 19:49). Eleazar shows up in verse 51 helping hand out the land by lot. Same crowd, different man getting the gift.

Caleb, a man from the tribe of Judah, does get his own land in this book, so I see why he came to mind. But he's not the one in this passage. Here, when they finished distributing the land, the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them (Joshua 19:49).

Not quite, friend. The text says the Israelites gave Joshua his inheritance "as the LORD had commanded" (Joshua 19:50). So there was a command from the LORD behind it. They weren't just doing him a favor on their own.
False is right, friend. The Israelites gave Joshua the city "as the LORD had commanded" (Joshua 19:50). So the LORD's command stands behind this gift. It wasn't just the people's idea.

He asked, friend. The Israelites gave him the city of Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim "as he requested" (Joshua 19:50). After handing out everyone else's land, the man had one request of his own. And he got it.

Eleazar, the priest, is part of the distribution, but the text doesn't say he picked this one. It says they gave Joshua the city "as he requested" (Joshua 19:50). So the choice came from Joshua himself.

explanations.answer: It was the last city left
explanations.explanation: Leftovers sound like a sad ending for a man who did all this work, friend. But the text says nothing about the last city. It says they gave him Timnath-serah "as he requested" (Joshua 19:50). He asked for it.
Rebuilds, friend. Joshua "rebuilt the city and settled in it" (Joshua 19:50). He didn't just move in and put his feet up. He got to work on the place first, and then he settled in.
Dividing is what the whole passage is about, so I see why it popped up. But for his own city, Joshua rebuilt it and settled in it (Joshua 19:50). The lots were for the tribes. His city got a rebuild.
Emptying would be a strange way to start a home, friend. The text says Joshua "rebuilt the city and settled in it" (Joshua 19:50). He built it up, then he moved in.

True, friend. Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families distributed these inheritances by lot to the tribes of Israel at Shiloh before the LORD (Joshua 19:51). Priest, leader and family heads all in on it. Everybody had a hand in it, and the LORD's presence was right there.

This one's true, friend. The text says Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families distributed the inheritances "by lot to the tribes of Israel at Shiloh before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting" (Joshua 19:51). That's a lot of hands on one job. And all of it happened right there in the LORD's presence.
